headline: Boats ran the warm edge all week — yellowfin and mahi to show for the fuel, marlin bite thinner
subhead: The bridge from the Gulf Stream is still stretched across Wilmington, and the fleet is still cashing checks on it — for now.
body_markdown:
If you're weighing whether to run to Wilmington this week, the call is troll first, chunk as backup, and don't leave the dock without a full tank plus reserve — because the run is still paying, but it's not a slam dunk anymore. The warm water bridge that's been sitting over the canyon for three-plus weeks is holding, and it's still the difference between a good trip and a long ride for nothing. Boats working the color change and current edges on the canyon are still connecting with yellowfin, mahi, and the occasional white marlin on classic black/purple and green/zucchini spreads pulled at 6 to 7 knots. Bluefin have been the soft spot in that mix all month — a few here and there, nothing you'd plan a trip around.

We flagged this pattern back on September 7th — said the pelagic bite would hold as long as the warm water stayed put, and that's exactly what's happened. The filament hasn't broken down, and the fleet's still finding fish on it. That's the good news. The thing to watch, and we said this too on the 11th, is any cold pinch working in from the north side of that warm tongue. Nothing in this week's reports says it's happened yet, but it's the kind of thing that shows up fast and without much warning — one day you're marking bait and color on the temp break, the next day it's shoved forty miles east and you're burning diesel to find it again.

For the guys running out of Cape May or Indian River, the math hasn't changed: it's a long day regardless of which way the fish are sitting, so the smart play is checking the latest SST imagery the morning of and picking your corner based on where that break is actually sitting, not where it was three days ago. The eddies coming off the Gulf Stream up here don't hold still, and burning fuel to a stale image is how you turn a break-even day into a losing one. When the break's tight and clean, troll it hard early — first light through midmorning has been the more consistent window this week, before the wind builds and the surface gets choppy enough to blur the temp line visually.

On the troll, the boats doing well are running a mixed spread — a couple of small green/machine and green/zucchini lures inside, black/purple or black/red further back, with a naked ballyhoo or two skipping on the shorter riggers for the mahi and white marlin. Yellowfin have been running mid-size, nothing giant, but consistent enough on the right pass through the break to make the day worthwhile. Mahi have been mixed in wherever there's floating structure — weed lines, debris, anything holding bait — and a few have come up nice, in the 15 to 20 pound range, on the flat lines.

Chunking has worked as a secondary play once the sun's up and the troll bite slows, particularly for the bigger yellowfin sitting deeper on the temp break. Butterflied bunker on a slow drift, fished on circle hooks with just enough weight to get it down through the first 30 to 40 feet, has drawn some quality bites for boats willing to sit and wait rather than keep running lines. It's not a fast bite — more a patience game — but when a bigger yellowfin decides to work the chunk slick, it's worth the wait. Worth noting: this is a better play once you've already marked fish on the troll and want to capitalize on them rather than a blind starting strategy.

White marlin have thinned out compared to a few weeks back, which tracks with where we are in the calendar — that bite typically tapers through mid-September as the migration starts sliding south and the fish spread out rather than holding tight to the canyon edges. If you're specifically hunting marlin, the better odds are still on the troll rather than the chunk, working the temp breaks with the naked ballyhoo and a spread of lures that gives a visual target without overcommitting bait.

Looking at the next few days, the pattern should hold if the warm water stays anchored where it's been sitting — that's the entire equation right now. If the filament stretches or narrows but stays intact, expect the yellowfin and mahi bite to keep producing on the same troll pattern, with chunking as the play once boats find concentrations worth sitting on. If a cooling push does work in from the north — and that's the wildcard we're watching after last week's flag — the smart move is checking fresh temp breaks the morning of rather than assuming the fish are still sitting where they were Tuesday. Fuel is the real cost here, not bait, so the boats making money on this run are the ones checking conditions hard before they leave the dock, not after they're forty miles out and guessing.
